name: Evidence Extraction Tables
title: Evidence Extraction Tables
answer: Evidence extraction tables are structured grids used in systematic reviews and evidence synthesis to record what each included study did, who it studied, what it measured, and what it found. They turn free text papers into comparable rows and columns so reviewers can see patterns, conflicts, and gaps. They sit between search and screening on one side and synthesis and reporting on the other. A table may cover study design, sample, intervention, comparator, outcomes, effect sizes, and risk of bias. The exact fields follow the review question and the protocol.

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are structured grids used in systematic reviews and evidence synthesis to record what each included study did, who it studied, what it measured, and what it found. They turn free text papers into comparable rows and columns so reviewers can see patterns, conflicts, and gaps. They sit between search and screening on one side and synthesis and reporting on the other. A table may cover study design, sample, intervention, comparator, outcomes, effect sizes, and risk of bias. The exact fields follow the review question and the protocol.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These tables run on spreadsheets, relational databases, or dedicated review platforms, often with a shared template and controlled vocabularies. Teams may use cloud documents for live collaboration, version history, and comments, or offline files for sensitive data. Some projects link each cell to a source location, such as a page, table, or paragraph in the paper. Data dictionaries and codebooks keep column meanings stable across reviewers. The infrastructure must support export to analysis software and long term archiving.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with a protocol and a draft extraction form, which is piloted on a few studies and revised. Reviewers extract independently, then compare entries and resolve differences by discussion or a third reviewer. Calibration exercises and regular checks keep agreement high. Each entry is tied to the original paper, and any calculated value is documented with its source. Automation can pre fill fields from PDFs or abstracts, but a human verifies every cell before it enters the final table.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance matter because extraction tables often reproduce facts and short phrases from copyrighted papers. Teams respect licence terms, keep personal data lawful and minimal, and avoid copying long passages. Provenance means each cell can be traced to a source, with versioned forms, audit trails, and clear authorship of decisions. Common risks include transcription errors, misclassification, duplicate rows, and bias in what gets extracted. Publishing the extraction form and codebook helps others check the work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward semi automated and living evidence tables, where natural language processing and large language models suggest extractions from new papers. Human reviewers still check those suggestions, because models can miss context, invent values, or misread a table. Common data elements and machine readable formats are making tables easier to share and merge across reviews. Evidence maps and linked data may let a single extraction feed multiple questions and updates. The main challenges are keeping provenance, managing rights, and preventing automation from hiding errors.
